So you're thinking of putting all your shared #python code into a Dockerfile, e.g.
COPY utils.py /shared_stuff

1) That code is not in a venv.
2) That is not a versioned package
3) docker build will break your code as be base image evolves
4) can't run unit test or execute your code
5) have to add utils.py to your code repo & .gitignore it

parts.contentHtml:
Any option that involves wheel files is correct.

But if you really want to shoot your self in the foot:
1) store utils.py in wikipedia. You really will never know what is there
2) store it in a cookie that you have use browser automation to access. It will be astonishing to maintenance devs
3) store it in bash history, it is the source control for bash, it can be source control for #python
4) store it in a random number generator, at one offset or another, there will be the bytes of utils.py

import System.Random
import Control.Concurrent

data Fish = Fish { x :: Int, y :: Int }

moveFish :: Fish -> IO Fish
moveFish (Fish x y) = do
dx <- randomRIO (-1, 1)
dy <- randomRIO (-1, 1)
return (Fish (x + dx) (y + dy))

displayFish :: Fish -> IO ()
displayFish (Fish x y) = do
putStrLn (replicate x ' ' ++ "🐟" ++ replicate (80 - x) ' ')

main = do
let fish = Fish 10 10
forever $ do
fish' <- moveFish fish
displayFish fish'
threadDelay 1000000

records.contentHtml: If you see some clever objection to something, think, what are the implications of that being a universal law. If you do nothing with the implications, maybe you're not engaging in moral reasoning, but some sort of feel-good project of getting angry at some people, but exempting yourself & your actions from any similar scrutiny. Usually this gets called arrogance, but I see it as aggressive status-quo maintenance. Engaging in our clever objection would mean us having to change our behavior.

I got this theory that a name is a shorthand way of saying "Act like the person who'd be named "X"- so if you said 'your name is Space Karen', you'd get whatever the cultural tropes are that are associated with that name.

Or maybe not! Explicit works better than subtle, so "Write like Jules Vernes" should work better than "Your name is now Jules Vernes"

records.contentHtml: @jamiemccarthy I had in mind how we use code from pypi without actually checking if it is from someone reliable (not malicious, writes good code, etc). There are some tools, namely `safety`, `bandit`, and so on that ex post facto tell you if a library is dodgy, but at point of installation, we trust it blindly. Also, when using `lib==*` we also trust that the latest package isn't now malicious (sometime it is).

I finally cleaned up and pushed openmock 2.2.0, which incorporate 2 pull request from the community. #opensearch

https://pypi.org/project/openmock/2.2.0/

Lessons learned
- Easier to fork a project that has a build script that goes beyond just unittests
- Libraries should do matrix builds, apps generally not, so it has to be a different build script
- gitlab actions makes it easy to see if your code is unnecessarily windows incompatible.

key = line of code
value = variable assigned there

#podman runs ephemeral containers and itself is ephemeral, much preferring to print `Error: invalid character '\x00' looking for beginning of value` rather than to pull, build or run images.

It will hose itself so bad every day that you need to run this

```
# rm -rf ~/.config/containers
# wsl --unregister podman-machine-default
podman machine stop
podman machine rm
podman machine init
podman machine start
```

3- Run on the treadmill at 11pm Friday
4- Realize the other guy is also running on treadmill at 11pm
5- Run faster
6- Stop #running at 11:59PM

My heart rate didn't return to normal until 2:30AM. But I won!

#pypi #markdown #python

Ever want to turn json into markdown? I wanted to and couldn't. So I made a python-to-markdown serialization library. Handles some but not all types.
```
>>> loads("- a\\n- b\\n - c\\n")
['a', 'b', 'c']
```
and
```
>>> dumps([1,2])
'- 1\\n- 2\\n'
```
https://pypi.org/project/markpickle/0.2.0/

@neurobashing Intelligence without sentience is a philosophical zombie. Qualia can't be proven, so it's an arm chair question. Sentience is one of the ways to define the boundaries of a moral community.

"Autonomous" was a good exploration of some of these themes.
https://www.amazon.com/Autonomous-Novel-Annalee-Newitz/dp/0765392070

@neurobashing No human knows if any other human is alive in the inside. We're making a choice to treat other humans as being the same as us because we know us and assume that the other similar to ourselves must be much the same. What counts as "the same as us" is a fuzzy match. If DNA is what counts, then AI is not in our moral community, no problems. If the ability to think like a human is what counts, than AI is in our moral community & people don't like expanding moral communities like that

# IT Jobs, a taxonomy

## Working class smart person
8 hours day, surge days at ship-to-prod times. Hard work, sweeping sand into the sea, infinite TODO-lists.

## Piece work
Work is so well defined a 3rd party contractor could do it, e.g. move datacenter to new building.

## Fireman work
Do nothing unless server is down. Then work around the clock to fix it.

## BS Job
Org is throwing people at the project with no clue what will work. Unclear goals & chaos, idle people for most of the year.

Hey javascript people. Here is how you handle a situation where you can't continue

```typescript
if (records.length === 0) {
throw Error('No records provided, cannot continue.')
}
```
Not a quiet early return, not adding a `?.1` question mark to every object with a property, not wrapping in a try/catch-blank catch body.

Of course there is a global error handler that is discarding all errors, so you gotta find that too & disable it.

records.contentHtml: Also, on the ChatGPT tag, I see people so upset at ChatGPT they say that it is incapable of saying anything true, which is a horrifying stance to take. If a insentient thing (a bot, or a book, or a thing) is incapable of expressing a true fact, then what is truth? Take away ability for truth to be stand alone an embodied in a text and what you have left is *authority*, things are true because the guy in charge says so.

- We don't know what is happening in unsubscribe(), maybe nothing
- The computer will be shut down, we will all die, and the universe will be cold and black and so should we really care about collecting the garbage early
- Out-of-memory will force garbage collection organically as the user reboots.

```json
{
"strictNullChecks": true,
"strictPropertyInitialization": true,
}

On a pre-existing code base, setting "neutral" default values is the way to go. In greenfield code, meaningful constructors, maybe.

Revealed preference is the economics idea that what people do is what people prefer. What #typescript and #javascript developers prefer as their main async pattern is a race... two async methods that both reference and modify the same data structure with no particular guarantees who changes it or reads it first.

All the other patterns have rich abstraction libraries, but this one doesn't.

#Angular testing styles

- testbed - set up complex dependency chains so you can verify html. Then ignore html anyhow by including CUSTOM_ELEMENTS_SCHEMA**.**
- no-test bed - fast, ignored HTML on purpose, you must be a master of mocking & spies
- cyprus - you gave up on unit testing just doing e2e
- storybook - make a mini-app for each component.
- real-http - Integration tests but not necessarily via a browser, uses real HttpClientModule

So far all of these are various degrees of pain.

records.contentHtml: Build servers were never meant to deal with the size of node_modules for hello world. Time to download 1GB from npm is about as slow as moving 1GB around a build server. If the cache has to move into and out of the build server, then at node_module scale, it stops speeding things up. Also, if the cache isn't local or stable, then even pnpm won't speed things up because pnpm's speed relies on the initial cache existing. Maybe if node_modules it was baked into the base docker image...

#Agile #Scrum un-#SAFe
Sprint velocity shouldn't be confused with a time card or itemized bill for tasks

Let's imagine it was. First off, it will be the worst, most inaccurate ever because you're making guesses about the unknowable future, not commitments. Real time cards are recorded *as it happens* for this reason.

Point estimates are self declared by individual contributors. If there are $ penalties to not reaching velocity, you merely keep your job if you hit velocity, lose your job if not

Sprint velocity shouldn't be confused with a time card or itemized bill for tasks

Let's imagine it was. First off, it will be the worst, most inaccurate ever because you're making guesses about the unknowable future, not commitments. Real time cards are recorded *as it happens* for this reason.

Point estimates are self declared by individual contributors. If there are $ penalties to not reaching velocity, you merely keep your job if you hit velocity, lose your job if not

Sprint velocity shouldn't be confused with a time card or itemized bill for tasks
Let's imagine it was. First off, it will be the worst, most inaccurate ever because you're making guesses about the unknowable future, not commitments. Real time cards are recorded *as it happens* for this reason.
Point estimates are self declared by individual contributors. If there are $ penalties to not reaching velocity, you merely keep your job if you hit velocity, lose your job if not

parts.contentHtml: When team velocity is treated as a 12 week pre-committed time card, itemized bill, then when a team member is out sick or quits or is fired, and the whole team is expected to meet the same velocity (because it was a pre-declared time card/contract to deliver) then the rest of the team picks up 40 hours of work per week until a replacement is hired. If that person was a specialist, then the other specialist gets to work 80 hours a week.

parts.contentHtml: Except the math doesn't work. I think this came about from someone thinking, "If you are a good moral person, you will live up to your agreements and you agree to 100 velocity points, so you will do what it takes to deliver 100 points." And for maybe 10% variations, sure, people will work late out of a sense of professionalism. But if you ask a honest person to jump 10 feet when the maximum one person can jump is 5, then they can't. Doesn't matter how honest or professional they are.

parts.contentHtml: So what is going to happen. Goodhart's law on perverse incentives is going to kick in. Those velocity points are self declared monopoly money. They're not objective. They are good planning tools as long as you don't give people an incentive to lie. To minimize the risk of the maximum loss, it is now rational for *developers* to plan for 50% slack or more. To squeeze out the last 10% of efficiency, you've cut output by 50% or more.

re: reddit & twitter killing off APIs
What if a company made an API (instead of App + Api) & agreed with all their customers to only ever sell the API, not to create competing consuming API apps. Then it would be safe to make a business based on an API. There would still be an economic incentive for one party to attempt to try to get more than their fair share of the total. But if the each company was legally prevented from doing the others, it would at least be a commercial suicide pact.

records.contentHtml: Is people using ChatGPT to think up malicious package names an new AI centric exploit? I'm skeptical. This is AI assisted typosquatting. Meat based LLMs are already `pip install` ing packages that they think exist but don't, e.g. everytime you install a module by name when the package name has nothing to do with the package. Making the LLM part go away still leaves you with the fact that `pip install` just does what you ask.

@prosewitch False positive/false negative rates are currently somewhere between 5% and over 50%. If you do lots & lots of tests, most (almost all) of the AI texts flagged as AI will be wrong, because at the moment, most text is human generated.

Comparison to a known person's normal writing is probably a better test.

If you work on a team & if a project isn't split into separate packages, over time all files/classes/modules will eventually import from all other files and all methods will have imports inside of them to get around cyclical imports.

Splitting into packages will make it impossible for child packages to import from parent packages.

At 96+ your sleeping with a environmental fever.
At 106 you got a medical emergency

Anyhow, f*k that s*t I don't care if CA is the home of Silicon Valley and Hollywood, I'm staying away.

I realize why I dislike "I got my tickets done, I can take the rest of the day/week off"-I mean, aside from the federal time card fraud crime part

- Everything's broken
- Our best code is still somewhat broken
- We fix it until we run out of time
-"I got my tickets done" is an arbitrary quitting time, it means "I worked until I didn't feel like working on it anymore"

There is an element of "definition of done" and did it pass process, but that is a fiction we project over the reality of coding

I'll have to keep tweeting this until it reaches the right people

How to break into tech
- Read the manual-"Learning Python", etc
- Have a side project on github
- Don't google questions/coding solutions in interviews
- Don't BS, be willing to say I don't know/remember.
- Play with your cards up (e.g. ask if you can google the syntax for mocking a return value)

If you object to one or more of the above, you need to think up an alternate way. Indignation, resentment-aren't job qualifications*

* by indignation, I mean, the common objections like
- "I can code in Javascript, I shouldn't have to demonstrate Python"
- "I don't owe the world my spare time for a public side project"
- "If it can be googled a candidate should need to know it"
- "BS? I don't BS. You're BS"
- "Looking up fizzbuzz on a 2nd monitor is about my right to privacy"

For the speed readers - you get to agree with some of these indignant feelings, but not all of them, or else a candidate becomes unevaluatable.

I'm reading up on longevity & paleontology (of mammals). My armchair theory of the day is: we get old and die because of our teeth. For literally billions of years, mammals create 2 sets of teeth for life (the have to fit together perfectly, so they are irreplaceable) Once your 2nd set are used up, you die. Everything else in your body evolved to work just well enough to last as long as your teeth.

Sharks (new teeth all the time) can live up to 400 years.

records.contentHtml:
#chagGPT plugins:
ChatGPT seems to have 2 store of knowledge- stuff you said in the prompt and stuff just ambient in its "brain". The "brain" has waaaay more stuff in it. The prompt is just info about your desires to encourage it to put out a good response.

EXLUDING TOOLS, the plugins are mostly prompt info, they don't give the bot more info for its brain. I think that is what embeddings are about, but I don't think most plugins are doing that.

W/o a plugin, the bot will say something from its full store of knowledge. Once it queries wikipedia or the web, it switches to summarization mode & summarizes that document. You really get this when the query returned something different from what the prompt was about. It just treat it like a topic change.

Anyhow. That's my 2c based on probably not enough experiments.

- car (burning gasoline)
- house (burning gas)

Leaving things like books, clothing, side walks as innocent consumption. But all of that is embodied fossil fuel usage.

Matt's health advice:
It is a game of odds, pull some levers and your odds get better.
Lifestyle is big, but at best you can go from 60-80 to 90 (years lived), or improve your health span.
Once you get cancer or dementia, you're toast. Many lifestyle factors can delay it.
Heart disease is excess calories, esp saturated fat & being sedentary (all 3) & is largely avoidable.
Cancer is what will kill you if something else doesn't kill you first.

I'm phasing out my usage of #pipenv in all my #python side projects. Why?
- Pipenv can't package.
- Pipenv will soon always lock (which is slow, if I have to, then might as well us poetry)
- Poetry lock speed is bearable if you set minimum versions on *everything*
- Poetry supports pyproject.toml
- Poetry works fine for both libraries & apps (Pipenv aims to solve the problem of apps, not libraries)
- I figure out how to handle poetry private repos. I never figured that out for pipenv

#ChatGPT is already famous for not being able to do a histogram of the letter in a word. But if you ask it to make up an (back)acronym, in my experience it usually can spell.

The best explanation if I've seen so far is that the tokens are encoded as if all languages were Chinese symbols, e.g. cat = 1564. ChatGPT's neurons doesn't directly know 1564 corresponds to c, a, t and is doing this by inference. But that doesn't explain why it can make up correct acronyms.

#ChatGPT is already famous for not being able to do a histogram of the letter in a word. But if you ask it to make up an (back)acronym, in my experience it usually can spell.
The best explanation if I've seen so far is that the tokens are encoded as if all languages were Chinese symbols, e.g. cat = 1564. ChatGPT's neurons doesn't directly know 1564 corresponds to c, a, t and is doing this by inference. But that doesn't explain why it can make up correct acronyms.

- APIs (must follow ToS, risk of getting flagged as bad & account closed),
- renting a cloud machine (high set up costs, maximum friction)
- running on ordinary CPUs with low memory (stupid LLM, glacial text generation)
- buy a new computer & tune model for that cpu

parts.contentHtml:
One pattern is you have to strategically hide tools. If I ask it to search pypi, screw that, I can do that directly. But if I ask it to suggest a package without tools, it will give me a mix of real and hallucinated packages. I have it use a tool to check if they really exist and then I get a good result.

Bing hyperfixates on the top 5 results from bing to the exclusion of its much vaster but more unreliable inner "knowledge" or whatever it is called-sometimes true, sometimes justified facts

records.contentHtml: #ChatGPT If you're coding bot interactions, one pattern is to code up TWO bots, the 2nd checks the first. If you ask the same bot, "hey, can you double check your answer?", you risk the bot doubling down because it thinks it is a good bot, or it rolls over & agrees to anything because it is a cooperative bot. The 2nd bot thinks it is reviewing someone else's text, and is willing to be a picky fault-finder, which is what we want.

re: housing is expensive
Well, the only solution is never build anything anywhere because someone might get rich from it or some rich person could move it that house.

We can't do anything for the poor because we hate the rich, nevermind that the communist revolution is not on the way. Far better to remain ideologically pure than to do something about the high cost of housing.

Also doesn't help that any price drop in housing wrecks everyone's retirement, so who knows who has honest objections.
